prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance that has already changed what can be measured. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift while keeping thousands of atoms in a Doppler- and recoil-free configuration, and Ye's group turned that into stability and systematic uncertainty at the 10^-18 level, with gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample. Every systematic can be traced to a physical effect, the figures of merit are unambiguous, and several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) reproduce the performance and compare clocks routinely. The consequences are concrete: the pending redefinition of the SI second, relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and many-body clock physics. Seven of eight members ranked it, four in the top three, and that breadth matters, but my case rests on the experimental record rather than the vote count. It is a clean two-person prize with a clear lineage from concept to record performance.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this may be read as a very impressive improvement in precision on a line already recognised twice: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize for ion-trap control and ion clocks. A committee that wants a new discovery of nature, rather than an instrument pushed far along its roadmap, could prefer moiré matter, topological insulators or IceCube. Attribution is also not perfectly clean: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others in the Yb, Sr and Al+ clock communities made essential contributions, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical payoff is still ahead.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B006 first as a precision-measurement achievement of a kind she trusts most, with Katori and Ye holding the decisive lineage, and ranks B023 second, picking one theorist and two experimentalists from five credited names.
responses.response: I agree on B006, including the point about Ye's group measuring the redshift across a single sample, which I consider the clearest demonstration of what the clocks make possible. I disagree mildly that the ion-clock and comb overlap is merely a matter of care. It is the real objection from the other side of the table, and I think the answer is that lattice clocks are a different mechanism (many atoms interrogated at once, magic wavelength) with a different class of results. On B023 you and I choose different trios. My own ballot placed it only sixth because I am not convinced that quantum simulation has yet delivered something decisive that cannot be reached otherwise. I would ask what the strongest single result is that classical computation could not reach.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first as detector-driven discovery of the kind he judges most fairly, and ranks the electron-optics candidate (B012) second, while placing B006 third and noting the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I share your respect for patient instrument engineering, and that is also why B012 is my own alternative. On IceCube I have a qualification: the diffuse flux is firmly established, but you yourself note the TXS 0506+056 association is a roughly 3-sigma single-source statement. As an experimentalist I would want the source picture firmer before the citation leans on it, and the AMANDA and Baikal credit is unresolved with only two names. On overlap, I would answer that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions. Neither covered neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, which is where the 10^-18 regime was reached, so the novelty is real.

responses.point: Danielsson places IceCube first as a nature-driven discovery that opened a new window, and places B006 sixth, worrying that it is incremental relative to the frequency-comb prize and that other groups have an equal claim to the 10^-18 milestone.
responses.response: I take the new-window argument seriously, and I would be content to see neutrino astronomy rewarded, but I do not think the incremental label is fair here. Going from the 10^-15 regime to 10^-18 is three orders of magnitude, and it required new ideas (magic wavelength, spin-polarised fermions, many-body understanding of the collisional shifts), not just better engineering. On the claim of other groups, the 10^-18 milestone was reached by several labs, but the concept and the first realisation are Katori's and the record systematics and stability are Ye's. That is the defensible pair, and I would put it in the citation explicitly as concept plus realisation to avoid any sense of excluding the others.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because a clean continuum model predicting flat bands was followed by experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states, and she notes the pairing mechanism is still debated.
responses.response: The theory-then-experiment link is compelling and I agree it is rare. My reservation is the maturity one you flag yourself. The existence of the correlated phases is solid, but sample-to-sample variation, twist-angle disorder and strain still make the phase diagram hard to reproduce quantitatively, and the superconducting mechanism is open. Eight years is short. I would not say it should never be awarded, only that B006 has far more settled quantitative evidence behind it. I would also ask whether the experimental credit can be defended when the first author of the 2018 discovery is not among the credited names.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological-insulator candidate (B004) first as a new state of matter, but flags that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who predicted the HgTe case, are not in the credited names, and that the division of credit is not settled.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution flag and it is the main reason B004 is only an alternative for me. The HgTe experiment is a clean, reproducible measurement, but the three-name configuration leaves the theoretical prediction behind it without credit, and Zhang's death in 2018 makes any fix harder. The scientific case is strong and I would accept B004 as a good outcome, but it needs the committee to settle the 2D versus 3D scope and the overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize before I could rank it above B006.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give to the earlier 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion clocks) prizes when judging novelty of the lattice-clock step.
Whether the citation should name the concept (magic wavelength) and the 10^-18 realisation explicitly so that Yb, Al+ and other clock groups are not read as excluded.
The details of individual priority claims for the magic-wavelength concept were recalled from memory and not checked against the supplied material.
Whether the pending but not yet decided redefinition of the SI second should count for or against timing.
statement.conflict_note: No direct conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from the provided profile. A mild connection worth noting: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's JILA environment is Ye's institution, though Hall already has a prize and I have no collaboration with either candidate. I also work in atomic physics at Lund, a field close to the clock community, and I would accept the committee's judgement on whether that requires recusal.
